INTRODUCTIONM

Large multi-engine aircraft typically have a power generation device attached to each engine accessory drive section. Together, the power generation devices provide power to all of the electrical and electronic components throughout the aircraft.
It would be very costly and dangerous to connect each electrical component directly to the power generation device.

To reduce costs, lighten the aircraft, and provide efficient power; aircraft are designed with power distribution systems that safely route power to electrical and electronic systems throughout the aircraft...

In this lesson you will learn about the types of aircraft power distribution systems used in large multi-engine aircraft. You will be able to define how they are designed, identify system components and explain their purpose, and describe how each type of system operates...
Let's begin our lesson on MULTI- ENGINE AIRCRAFT POWER DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS.

SPLIT-BUS POWER DISTRIBUTION
DISCUSSION

Multi-engine aircraft generate power for all electrical and electronics systems using a generator or alternator mounted on each engine. The Power Distribution System routes power to all of the electrical and electronic components on the aircraft.

Basic power generation systems connect the engine power generation device to a main bus. From there, the power is distributed to the aircraft systems through circuit breakers, relays, and specialized busses...

One type of Multi-engine power distribution system is the Split-bus Power Distribution system. This system is configured much like several independent basic generation systems. Each generating device powers its own distribution system. The various electrical systems are "split" between the independent busses.....
Split-bus power generation systems are very common on twin engine transport aircraft like the B737, B757, B767, B777, DC9, MD80, and A320.

The split bus distribution system connects each generator to one main bus, but never to both busses at the same time. This eliminates the need for generator paralleling since the two sources never power the same bus...

Typically, number one (#1) loads are connected to the #1 Main Bus and number two (#2) loads are connected to the #2 Main Bus. For example, the #1 Flight Director system would be connected to the #1 bus...
Common loads that do not have a second redundant system, such as Lighting, Landing Gear, and Radar systems are distributed between the two busses so that they draw equal loads from each bus...

There are two classifications of power distribution busses; the Non-Shed Bus, often called the Essential bus, and the Shed Bus, often called the Non-essential bus. Non-essential busses are connected to the Main bus by Shed Relays...

Before we learn about how a split-bus power distribution system works, let's look at some of the components that make up the system. As we learned, each split bus system is powered by a generator or alternator...

In most large aircraft, an AC brushless generator provides the power. Each generator is connected to a constant speed drive system to ensure a frequency of 400 Hz.

Similar to the DC bus of small aircraft, the AC bus is an electrical power distribution point where several circuits are connected. It is often a solid metal strip having a number of terminals installed on it that allow connection to the circuits...

The main distinction of an AC bus is that it has a bus bar for each phase of the AC signal. To keep block diagrams simple, drawings typically show the phases as one line with three slashes for three phase power and a line with one slash for single phase power. DC power will have no slashes...

On modern split bus systems, a Generator Breaker (GB), connects the generator to the associated bus. GB 1 connects the #1 generator to the #1 Main bus and GB 2 connects the #2 generator to the #2 Main bus...

The Generator Breaker is a heavy duty power relay used to control high voltages. The contacts of the generator breaker are thick so the GB is capable of handling high levels of current. The GB has three separate contacts, one for each phase, and uses low voltage DC to control it...

The Generator Breaker, is controlled by the Generator Control Unit (GCU) and/or the Bus Controller. It automatically disconnects the generator from its associated bus during engine shutdown or generator failure.It can also disconnect the generator when commanded to do so from the pilot using a switch in the cockpit.....
The Generator Breaker can also disconnect the generator when commanded to do so from the pilot using a switch in the cockpit.

The Bus Tie Breakers (BTB) are primarily used to connect Main Bus #1 and Main Bus #2 to external power or auxiliary power unit power. On some aircraft split bus systems, the BTB is also used to connect the # 1 and # 2 busses together during a generator failure...
Bus Tie Breakers are controlled by a bus controller or electrical panel switches in the cockpit..

During normal Transfer Bus system operation, the GCU allows power to be supplied to associated transfer bus through the closed contacts of the Generator Breakers (GB) and the Transfer Relays....

Since both generators are on line, power is also provided to the non-essential or shed bus through the Transfer Relays. As long as the generators are operating within normal parameters, the Transfer Bus system will continue to operate in this configuration...
During an engine or generator failure the associated cockpit generator light would begin to flash red or otherwise give an indication of a failed generation system.

During a #2 generator failure, for example, the #2 GCU will sense a problem and disconnect the faulty generator from the power distribution system. It does this by removing DC control power from the #2 GB. At the same time, the #2 GCU will remove DC control power from the #2 Transfer Relay...

Notice that when the #2 Transfer Relay opens, both non-essential busses lose power. The #2 non-essential bus loses power because its associated generator failed and #1 non-essential bus loses power by the opening of the #2 Transfer Relay...

Instantaneously, when the #2 Transfer Bus opens, power from the #1 Main bus powers the #2 Transfer Bus through the normally closed (when un-powered) contacts of the #2 Transfer Relay. This happens in a micro-second from when the generator fails...

The non-essential busses will continue to be disconnected until another power source is available. If in flight, the Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) can be started to provide power to the #2 side of the distribution system. Let's see how that works...
When the APU is started and the APU GCU senses correct power, the APU GCU DC control power will close the APU GB and apply APU AC power to the #1 and #2 BTB's.
Once power reaches the #2 BTB, the bus controller will automatically close the #2 BTB and energize the #2 Transfer Relay. APU AC power will be routed to the #2 Main Bus and the #2 Transfer Busss

As APU power is being routed to the #2 Transfer Bus, it is also making its way back to the #2 non-essential bus. Since the #2 Transfer Relay is once again energized, power is also restored to the #1 non-essential bus from the #1 Main Bus...

On the ground, with engines shut down, the Transfer Bus Split Bus system can use either the APU or an External Power connection to power the aircraft systems. If External Power is used, the External Power Monitor ensures that the power from the external source is correct before allowing it on to the aircraft...

If correct power is ready, a green light in the cockpit will illuminate. An "Ext Pwr" switch in the cockpit sends a signal to the bus controller which closes the #1 and #2 BTB's and energizes the #1 and #2 Transfer Relays. Power is then routed to all busses...

1. Multi-engine aircraft generate power for all electrical and electronic systems using alternators or generators mounted on each engine accessory gearbox. Typically, large commercial twin engine aircraft use a Split Bus Power Distribution system.
2. A Split Bus Power Distribution System divides the loads evenly among both generators. Each generator is responsible for its own individual distribution bus system.
3. There are many types of Split Bus systems, however, two types are most common; the Line Contactor Controlled Bus and the Transfer Bus systems..s own individual distribution bus system.
4. Line Contactors are used in many Split bus Power Distribution Systems to distribute power to the main busses. and the Transfer Bus systems..s own individual distribution bus system.

5. During normal operation the line contactors, controlled by the GCU, are closed to allow each generator to power an associated bus. When one generator fails, the line contactor automatically routes power from the good system to the failed system....

6. Transfer Bus Split Bus Power Distribution systems use Transfer Relays to route power to the Transfer and Non- Essential busses. When one generator fails, the Transfer Relay sheds non-essential loads and provides power from the good Main Bus to the failed Transfer Bus...

DISCUSSION
Multi-engine aircraft with three or four engines, use a Parallel Bus distribution system. The DC10, L1011, B727, and early models of the B747 all use a parallel bus power distribution configuration.

Like the Split Bus system, during normal operations the Parallel Bus system ties each generator to a unique bus. The difference is that all busses are connected together.

To connect all of the busses together, the Parallel Bus system employs a Tie Bus, also called the Synchronizing Bus. The Tie Bus is common to all generators so each generator must be at the same voltage, phase, and frequency at all times...
We will look at Transfer Bus systems in detail in the next section.
During normal operation, each generator powers its own bus through the associated Generator Breaker (GB) and contributes to the Tie Bus through its Bus Tie Breaker (BTB).
In the event that a generator fails, the Generator Control Unit (GCU), sensing the faulty condition, will open the (GB) for the faulty generator and isolate it from its bus.
Notice that the Bus Tie Breaker (BTB) for the #3 system does not open. It allows the Bus Tie power to continue powering the #3 Bus.
To relieve the remaining operational generators of the extra load, the crew can elect to start the APU and direct its generator output to assist in powering the Tie Bus. .
When the APU generator is up to speed, the APU GCU will close the APU GB and add its power to the Tie Bus.

As with most aircraft power distribution systems, the pilot can elect to reduce the load on the system by turning off non-essential equipment or opening the shed bus. On some aircraft each generator bus will have a non-essential load shed bus connected to it and on other aircraft a single non-essential bus is connected to the Tie Bus.....

Another possible condition in a Parallel Bus system is a Bus short. If one of the individual busses senses a short to ground in any of its supporting systems, the associated GB and BTB will open isolating the bus from the rest of the distribution system...
In a bus short condition, those system loads unique to the faulted bus cannot be recovered, even if the APU generator is brought on line.

Providing external power to an aircraft configured with a Parallel Bus system is very similar to the Split bus system. In fact, most service personal do not know which type of system is actually powering the aircraft when they connect external power...

1. Parallel Bus Distribution Systems are utilized on large Multi- engine aircraft designed with 3 or 4 engine-driven generators. These aircraft include the DC10, L1011, B727, and early versions of the B747.
2. Like the Split Bus system, the Parallel Bus system ties each generator to an associated bus during normal operations. This bus is called the Tie Bus.
3. If a generator fails, the generator's GCU opens the Generator Breaker and removes it from its bus. The failed generator's bus is immediately powered by the remaining generators via the Tie Bus..
4. The Tie Bus provides APU and external power to each bus during engine out operations. The Generator Breakers open during external power operations to protect the generators...
5. If an individual bus experiences a short, both the Generator Breaker and the Bus Tie Breaker for that bus will open and isolate the fault from the generator and Tie Bus.

6. Four engine aircraft, such as the B747-400, are often designed with a Modified Split Bus power distribution system. The Modified Split Bus system combines the Split Bus and the Parallel Bus Systems.

7. During normal operations the #1 and #2 generators are paralleled together and power their individual busses and a shared Tie Bus. The #3 and #4 generators are paralleled together and power their individual busses and a shared Tie Bus that is isolated from the #1 and #2 Tie Bus.

8. If one generator fails, its paralleled generator will provide power to its bus. If both generators on a side fail, a Split System Breaker will open and provide power to both failed generators' busses.

EXPERIMENT
In this experiment, you will look at the basic operation of a Split- Bus Distribution system. By understanding this operation, troubleshooting of a faulty system can be quick and effective.
The circuits are mounted on two circuit cards. The controls, components and indicators represent different sections of an aircraft Split-Bus system.
Pick up and examine the PC130-735 card. This card is the AC to DC generator system which provides two balanced DC voltages. We will be using both voltage sources for this experiment...
Switches S1 and S2 are used to turn on and off the output of the generators. The output we will be using is two 12 volt DC sources.
The PC130-736 card is the Split-Bus Distribution system. Pick it up and examine it.
There are seven different busses represented on this card. The bus to the far left is the battery bus. This bus connects the battery output to the generator 2 and emergency busses.
S2 and S3 are the switches used to distribute the power from the battery. Remember, the battery should only be used to start the aircraft or when the aircraft generators fail.
The next two busses, bus 1 and bus 2, are the generator busses. The input to these busses is the output from the generators. Notice that there is a switch between the two busses.
In normal operation this switch should be in the NC (not connected) position. This in effect separates the two busses from each other.
The only time the busses would need to be connected is if one of the generators became faulty and were disconnected from the system.

Switch S1 is a non-essential disconnect switch. This removes all power from the non-essential loads. This is important when power is limited. Remember, the non-essential bus applies power to loads that are not necessary for safe flight.

The second bus connects to the essential and emergency busses. This is the most important bus of the Split-Bus Distribution system. The battery switch connects or disconnects battery power to this bus.

The emergency bus connects directly to the essential busses. This bus can be powered by the generator bus or directly from the battery through S3. If a generator bus becomes damaged, this is an alternate route for power.
Also seen on the card are representations of DC to AC static inverters. Some loads on aircraft require AC power and these devices convert the DC to AC from the generator bus.
Remember, all of the components on these cards are representations of aircraft relays and breakers which would be controlled in flight by a flight computer.

5. Set S3 to ON, and set S2 to OFF........................
Now power is being applied to the emergency bus from the battery bus instead of through the generator bus. This is important for emergency situations where the generator bus can't be used.
It is also important to note the diode connected from the generator bus to the essential load. A diode only allows power to flow in one direction.
For this reason, the generator bus can power the essential loads, but the emergency power can't power the generator bus. This allows the emergency bus to be powered by multiple sources independently.
Both of the generators should have become active again. The system is now being powered by the generators and the battery can be charged.
Now the system is working properly. It is important to remember that these switches you have set manually would be controlled by a computer located in an aircraft.
Power can be limited when a generator failure(s) occur. This means only necessary loads receive power to extend the amount of time backup power can be used.
We have seen how a power distribution system can be designed to control the flow of power effectively between sources and loads.
Remember, this experiment has introduced you to the idea of a Split- Bus system. Most aircraft will have very intricate systems that run off of these same principles.
